claim: In MTDSim every attack action and every deployment takes simulated time, counted in seconds.
quote: DiscreteEventSimulation(DES)involvessimulatingtimeforeverytime-consuming action in an event to integrate the time domain into the simulator. ... MTD technique Average Duration (s) Standard Deviation
locator: Sec. 4.5, p. 30 printed (PDF p. 31); Table 3, p. 33 printed (PDF p. 34)
issue: Holds for MTDSimTime, Zhang's extension of MTDSim: time for every time-consuming action, deployments timed in seconds. Zhang hedges to 'time-consuming' actions and gives times only for the three attack phases, not scan host, enum host or scan neighbour; the dissertation's attack-action durations come from tay2024code (U0120), so the sentence leans on Zhang only for the principle.

claim: A deployment takes from 20 s to 110 s to complete, depending on the mechanism.
quote: Table 3: MTD Execution Time MTD technique Average Duration (s) Standard Deviation CompleteTopologyShuffle 110 0.5 IPShuffle 100 0.5 OSDiversity 80 0.5 DAP_OSDiversity 80 0.5 ServiceDiversity 70 0.5
issue: Zhang's range is 70 s to 110 s, for four of the seven mechanisms (plus DAP OS diversity, which the dissertation does not run). The 20 s lower bound, and any time for host topology shuffle, port shuffle and user shuffle, is not in Zhang; it must come from the code. Zhang's values are also means (SD 0.5), not fixed times. A wrong number attributed to the supervisor's student's thesis.
fix_text: 'takes from 20\,s to 110\,s to complete, depending on the mechanism \citep{zhang2023}' -> cite the code release (tay2024code, constants) for the 20 s to 110 s range, keeping zhang2023 only for the four mechanisms it times (70 s to 110 s)

claim: The seven MTD mechanisms come from Brown's pool, added to by Zhang.
quote: Inthepreviouswork[17], sevenMTDtechniqueswereimplemented. Forthisstudy, we selected four techniques ... Additionally, we introduce a newly implemented MTD technique in Section 4.3.1.5. ... the newly implemented MTD technique seeks to improveOSDiversity by solving the Diversity Assignment Problem (DAP) [38].

Nothing in the table was 'added to by Zhang', so the caption misattributes.
fix_text: delete ', added to by Zhang~\citep{zhang2023},' from the caption

claim: The random, alternative and single deployment strategies follow a schedule, so they are proactive.
quote: three specific MTD execution schemes are introduced in this work: random execution, alternative execution, and simultaneous execution. MTDSimTime utilises time-based proactive MTD execution schemes with various execution strategies. Since these MTD techniques are triggered periodically and do not have reactive concerns, they are all implemented as time-based proactive schemes.
issue: Zhang calls random, alternative and simultaneous periodic and proactive. 'Single' is not one of Zhang's schemes: it is the single-MTD evaluation condition (Sec. 5.1), which Zhang does not classify. Right reasoning, one item outside the source's list.
fix_text: 'The random, alternative and single deployment strategies' -> 'The random and alternative deployment strategies \citep{zhang2023}, and the single one, ...' or keep with the reasoning marked ours for single

claim: Three of the four deployment strategies (random, alternative, single) are from Zhang.
quote: three specific MTD execution schemes are introduced in this work: random execution, alternative execution, and simultaneous execution. ... The random execution scheme was used in previous work [17].
locator: Sec. 4.3.2, p. 23 printed (PDF p. 24); Sec. 4.3.2.1, p. 24 printed (PDF p. 25)
issue: Zhang's three are random, alternative and simultaneous; the table's third, single, is Zhang's single-MTD evaluation condition, not one of his schemes, and Zhang credits random to Brown [17]. Only alternative originates with Zhang. A supervisor who knows Zhang's three would notice the swap.

claim: A run ends when the attacker compromises more than 80 % of the hosts.
quote: we set the terminating condition for the simulation as the NCR reaching 0.8 and run the simulation 100 times for each variable set ... only the first attack scenario is selected to be refactored and simulated in MTDSimTime.
locator: Sec. 5, p. 32 printed (PDF p. 33); Sec. 4.4.1.1, p. 27 printed (PDF p. 28)
issue: Zhang ends at NCR 'reaching 0.8' (at least 80 %), not 'more than 80 %', and only in the general scenario, the only one Zhang ran. Table 2.2 (U0136) itself says '80 % of the hosts compromised', so the two disagree. If 'more than' is the code's strict comparison (attack_operation.py), that is the code, not Zhang. Session-drafted.
fix_text: 'more than 80\,\%' -> '80\,\%' (or keep 'more than' and cite the code for the strict threshold)

claim: An exploit of a vulnerability the attacker has exploited before takes half the time.
quote: In terms of the learning capabilities, the attack model is designed to halve the exploitation time spent on the vulnerabilities that were exploited in the previous attack operations conducted on previous hosts.
locator: Sec. 4.4.3 and Eq. 2, p. 30 printed (PDF p. 31)
issue: Holds; Eq. 2 halves the (1 - ACv) x TAexploit term for exploited vulnerabilities. Zhang scopes it to vulnerabilities exploited 'on previous hosts', which the sentence's 'before' covers.

claim: Each disruption costs the attacker a confusion penalty of about 20 s.
quote: The adversary in the simulator is designed to take a time penalty to simulate the confusion caused by MTD. The time penalty is assigned each time the attack event is interrupted or stopped by MTD.
issue: The penalty and 'each disruption' hold. The value '20 s' is nowhere in Zhang: not in the text, Table 3, or Figures 6-7 (checked as images). The tex comment traces it to constants.py:147, i.e. the code. A number attributed to Zhang that Zhang does not give.
fix_text: 'a confusion penalty of about 20\,s \citep{zhang2023}' -> 'a confusion penalty \citep{zhang2023} of about 20\,s \citep{tay2024code}'

claim: A deployment never takes back a compromised host.
quote: It is assumed that the compromised hosts will always stay compromised and can be recognised by the adversary immediately upon regaining access, regardless of any network changes made by MTD techniques.
issue: Holds, as a stated modelling assumption of Zhang's ('It is assumed'). The sentence states it as a fact about MTDSim, which is fine for a simulator description.

claim: A deployment never takes back a stolen credential.
quote: After compromising a host, the adversary gains access to all of its users, which they use to launch credential-stuffing attacks on other hosts in the network.
issue: Zhang says the attacker gains a compromised host's users but says nothing about credentials surviving a deployment; Zhang's MTDSimTime has no user shuffle (four mechanisms selected, Sec. 4.3.1). The credential half of an absence claim (R5) rests on the code, not Zhang. The uncited tail ('loses only the progress it must repeat', 'a topology shuffle also rebuilds its visible subgraph') is partly echoed by Zhang's 'restart the attack action from Phase 1' but the subgraph rebuild is not in Zhang; it reads as ours.
fix_text: 'a compromised host or a stolen credential \citep{zhang2023}' -> 'a compromised host \citep{zhang2023} or a stolen credential' (credential persistence from the code, tay2024code)

quote: Table 2: Network Properties Network Nodes Density Endpoints Layers 1 25 0.093 3 4 2 50 0.052 5 4 3 75 0.040 7 4 4 100 0.043 10 4 ... run the simulation 100 times for each variable set
locator: Table 2 and Sec. 5, p. 32 printed (PDF p. 33)

claim: Zhang's column: attack scenario general; run ends at 80 % of the hosts compromised.
quote: only the first attack scenario is selected to be refactored and simulated in MTDSimTime. ... we set the terminating condition for the simulation as the NCR reaching 0.8
locator: Sec. 4.4.1.1, p. 27 printed (PDF p. 28); Sec. 5, p. 32 printed (PDF p. 33)

claim: Zhang's column: deployment interval exponential, mean 50; 100; 150; 200 s.
quote: this work proposes using an exponential distribution to simulate theMTD Intervalin order to enhance the accuracy of the simulation. ... fourMTD Intervals, ranging from 50 to 200 seconds
locator: Sec. 4.3.4, p. 26 printed (PDF p. 27); Sec. 5, p. 32 printed (PDF p. 33); levels from Figure 8 panel titles, PDF p. 35 (checked as image)

claim: Defender-side effectiveness metrics measure the network's security, such as NCR (NCR as a defender-side effectiveness metric, per Zhang).
quote: we use Network Compromise Ratio (NCR) as the simulation checkpoint to evaluate MTD techniques and their combinations. NCR is the ratio of compromised hosts to the total number of hosts in the network. It helps us measure the effectiveness of our MTD techniques by measuring the time it takes for the adversary to compromise a certain proportion of hosts in the network.
issue: Zhang defines NCR but uses it as a checkpoint (the stopping threshold for MTTC), not as a measured outcome, and never classifies it as defender-side or as measuring 'the network's security'. The defender-side placement is Cho's frame applied by the dissertation. Session-drafted.
fix_text: 'such as network compromise ratio (NCR) \citep{zhang2023}' -> 'such as network compromise ratio (NCR), defined by Zhang \citep{zhang2023}' or keep with the placement owned as ours

claim: NCR is a defender-side effectiveness metric, sourced to Zhang.
quote: we use Network Compromise Ratio (NCR) as the simulation checkpoint to evaluate MTD techniques and their combinations. NCR is the ratio of compromised hosts to the total number of hosts in the network.
issue: As U0207: Zhang defines NCR and uses it as the terminating checkpoint, not as an effectiveness metric in its own right; the defender-side cell is the dissertation's classification.

claim: MTTC is an attacker-side effectiveness metric used by Zhang.
quote: Another static metric widely used is Mean Time to Compromise (MTTC), which measures the time it takes for an attacker to compromise a target host on the network [4]. ... Inthisstudy, MTTCisselected as the primary evaluation metric in the simulator
issue: Holds. Zhang adds that 'From the defender's perspective, MTTC can also be interpreted as MTTF', so the side is not exclusive, but the attacker-side cell is defensible.

claim: MTDSim's baseline attacker, as described in Section 2.2.3, is from Brown and Zhang.
quote: The adversary model in the simulation always follows a sequence of attack actions to identify and compromise hosts within the simulated network. ... only the first attack scenario is selected to be refactored and simulated in MTDSimTime.
issue: Holds as a lineage attribution with brown2023 beside it. Zhang's attacker runs only the general scenario and merges port scan with the credential attack (Phase 1), so the two-scenario attacker of Section 2.2.3 is Brown's, with Zhang's time additions. Section 2.2.3 also attributes the 20 s penalty and the 20-110 s range to Zhang (U0126, U0082), which Zhang does not give.

claim: Baseline attacker row cites Brown and Zhang, year 2023; marks are the dissertation's scores.
issue: Year holds. The marks are the dissertation's judgement, not claims about Zhang. One tension a supervisor may raise: Learn. is scored none, while Zhang names the exploit halving 'learning capabilities' (Sec. 4.4.3). The dissertation's Table 3.2 definition (patterns of past MTD deployments) excludes it, and U0269 explains this, so the mark is defensible.

claim: An exploit of a vulnerability it has exploited before takes half the time; the attacker keeps vulnerabilities.
quote: In terms of the learning capabilities, the attack model is designed to halve the exploitation time spent on the vulnerabilities that were exploited in the previous attack operations conducted on previous hosts.
issue: Holds.

claim: The baseline attacker has no learning (in a sentence citing Zhang for the halving).
quote: For the adversary side, Phase 2 can be affected by the learning capabilities and confusion of the adversary. In terms of the learning capabilities, the attack model is designed to halve the exploitation time
issue: Zhang calls this exact mechanism the attacker's 'learning capabilities'. The sentence cites Zhang for the mechanism while saying 'It has no learning'; the 'but' clause and the Table 3.2 definition make the judgement ours and defensible, but a reader who knows Zhang (the supervisor) sees the source's own label inverted without acknowledgement.
fix_text: 'It has no learning: an exploit' -> 'It has no learning: what Zhang calls learning is that an exploit' (or keep, with the reason recorded)

claim: NCR's source is Zhang (metrics table).
quote: we use Network Compromise Ratio (NCR) as the simulation checkpoint to evaluate MTD techniques and their combinations. NCR is the ratio of compromised hosts to the total number of hosts in the network.
issue: Zhang defines the ratio but uses it as a stopping checkpoint (fixed at 0.8 when every run ends), never as an outcome averaged over runs as Eq. (ncr) does. The same table marks adapted metrics 'this dissertation, after [...]'; NCR as an end-of-run outcome is such an adaptation.

claim: MTTC's source includes Zhang (metrics table).
quote: Another static metric widely used is Mean Time to Compromise (MTTC), which measures the time it takes for an attacker to compromise a target host on the network [4].
issue: Zhang's definition is itself cited to Cho et al. [4] (cho2020); Zhang is a user, not an origin, of MTTC. Harmless beside mcqueen2006 as the lineage's use, but not a definitional source.

claim: NCR is the share of the hosts the attacker has compromised when a run ends, averaged over runs.
quote: NCR is the ratio of compromised hosts to the total number of hosts in the network. ... we set the terminating condition for the simulation as the NCR reaching 0.8
issue: The ratio is Zhang's. 'When a run ends' (where the cite sits) is not: in Zhang every run ends when NCR reaches 0.8, so end-of-run NCR is constant by construction and never measured. The cite placement invites the reading that Zhang reads NCR at the end of a run.
fix_text: move '\citep{zhang2023}' to after 'that the attacker has compromised' (before 'when a run ends')

claim: MTTC is the mean time from the start of a run to the attacker reaching its goal, over the runs in which it does.
quote: Another static metric widely used is Mean Time to Compromise (MTTC), which measures the time it takes for an attacker to compromise a target host on the network [4]. ... Figure 8 presents the average time for the adversary to compromise 80% nodes of the target network for each MTD technique
locator: Sec. 3.4, p. 16 printed (PDF p. 17); Sec. 5.1, p. 33 printed (PDF p. 34)
issue: Zhang's written definition is borrowed from Cho [4] (secondary), and Zhang's operational MTTC is time to 80 % NCR, not to a target host. 'Over the runs in which it does' (conditioning on success) is not in Zhang, whose runs all end at 0.8 NCR. The tex comment says ruling H1 reads MTTC 'at a target host, Zhang's written definition'; that written definition is Cho's.
fix_text: keep \citep{mcqueen2006, zhang2023} on 'the mean time ... reaching its goal'; mark 'over the runs in which it does' as ours (or cite cho2020 for the definition)
